# Super Secret Notes by GaussRun

> A note you cannot afford to lose, saved in many independent places, recoverable anywhere with a
> vault name plus passphrase. Every note is copied to a dozen free hosts that need no signup, run by
> different people, so losing one host (or several) loses nothing. Before a note leaves the device it
> is encrypted twice, and each host adds its own layer. Works in the browser and with the
> `super-secret-notes` command line tool (same format).

Site: {{SITE_URL}}/
How it works (full, with sources): {{SITE_URL}}/how-it-works/
Source (AGPL-3.0-or-later): https://github.com/GaussRun/super-secret-notes
Command line tool: `super-secret-notes` (Node.js 24), same format as the web app.

## What it is for

- A secret note that must not vanish (recovery codes, a seed phrase backup hint, the wifi
  password): it is copied to many independent, free services at once, and check / repair find and
  fix damaged or missing copies.
- Moving a note from a public computer to a phone: make a throwaway vault in "public computer
  mode" (nothing is stored in that browser), write the note, scan a QR code with the phone.

## How it works

- Redundancy: by default PrivateBin pastebins (3), CryptPad accounts derived from the vault, Nostr
  relays (4) and Blossom blob servers (3); MEGA, Proton Drive, Filen and Fileverse are opt-in in the
  command line tool. Reads use the first copy that passes every check. An encrypted index lists the
  notes, where each copy lives and when each was last verified.
- Layer 1 (ours): age (https://age-encryption.org/v1, typage library): X25519, HKDF-SHA-256 and
  ChaCha20-Poly1305 key wrap; the note is ChaCha20-Poly1305 in 64 KiB chunks.
- Layer 2 (ours): AES-256-GCM with keys derived by HKDF-SHA256 from a random 32-byte master key;
  the blob id is bound as AAD. Code: overkill/cli/src/crypto.js in the repository.
- Layer 3 (each host): PrivateBin AES-256-GCM (key via PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, 100,000 iterations, key in
  the URL fragment); CryptPad XSalsa20-Poly1305 plus Ed25519 signatures; Nostr NIP-44 v2 (secp256k1
  ECDH, HKDF-SHA256, ChaCha20, HMAC-SHA256, padding); Blossom servers store bytes unchanged (BUD-02),
  so the tool adds its own extra AES-256-GCM layer there.
- Retention: PrivateBin pastes use "never" expiry; Nostr relays and Blossom servers promise none, so
  their copies are treated as possibly gone 120 days after publishing and republished (the tool's
  policy, not the hosts' promise).
- The web app is a static site with a strict Content-Security-Policy and no server of its own; it
  talks to the hosts directly from the browser.

## Recovery

- By name and passphrase: a scrypt-derived key finds a small encrypted record on Nostr relays,
  which leads to the encrypted vault file and from there to everything else.
- By the printed recovery kit (the age identity and master key), as a backstop.
- The passphrase can be saved by a password manager (vault name = username). New vaults get a
  generated six-word passphrase (about 77 bits).

## Security caveats

- The encrypted vault file is public on purpose, so the passphrase is the whole security: keep the
  generated one, or use one at least as strong.
- Lose the passphrase and the recovery kit and the notes are gone; nobody can reset anything.
- Whoever serves the web page could change it: for anything important, build and serve it
  yourself or use the command line tool.
- A public computer may log keystrokes or record the screen: use a throwaway vault there and
  change anything important afterwards. A QR code with the vault in it opens the vault for anyone
  who sees it.
- Free hosts promise little retention; run `check` now and then, and `repair`.
